1.pericope_label: Hold not thy peace, O God of my praise; for the mouth of the wicked is opened against me

debates.q: Against whom are the imprecations directed?

sides.view: Judas, and through him those who hated Christ then and since
Christ is the true speaker, David being a typical character; the Jewish nation is also in view
Primarily David’s betraying counsellor; if prophetic, the Jewish state rather than a man
One person, but who cannot be determined — the Edomite or the Benjamite, we do not know

debates.q: What does the clause rendered I give myself unto prayer say?

sides.view: Only and I prayer; the Chaldee and the versions supply but I pray
A known compression, and the context indicates prayer for the enemies themselves

outliers.view: Proposes that the curses may be the enemies’ execrations against David rather than his against them, removing the imprecations from the psalmist’s mouth
Decline to name the enemy at all, and find neither the late marks nor the older echoes that would date the psalm

6.pericope_label: Set thou a wicked man over him: and let Satan stand at his right hand

debates.q: Is the adversary of the sixth verse a name or a common noun?

sides.view: A common noun — let an adversary stand at his right hand, and let him be thwarted
The personal adversary, into whose hands the betrayer was given
An accuser, standing where accusers stood in the Jewish courts

debates.q: What is the office another is to take?

sides.view: Superintendence or oversight; the technical rendering has bred a cheap joke about the first bishop
Some post of power and influence
The apostleship, cut short so that his days were few beside his fellows

outliers.view: Dismantles the witticism that the first bishop was bishop Judas, and adds that Judas was no traitor at the time he was appointed
Reports that Calvin knew this psalm used as a curse against neighbours by friars, and calls the practice a detestable sacrilege

11.pericope_label: Let the extortioner catch all that he hath; and let the strangers spoil his labour

debates.q: Why is the mother named beside the father?

sides.view: Completeness of vengeance, and perhaps an allusion to a foreign descent if the curses are a quotation
Not the patriarchs but the Amorites and Hittites, or the ancestors who killed the prophets
Literally, in the expulsion, taxation and poverty of the Jews under Rome
In the Roman siege, and possibly in the debts of Judas
They express a general Hebrew principle: ruin falls on the posterity if not the sinner

outliers.view: Documents the fulfilment from a Roman satirist, quoting the picture of Jews camped beyond the city gate whose whole wealth was a basket and a wisp of hay
Reports a reading on which this whole section is a quotation of curses spoken against David by one of his revilers, and finds the mention of the mother evidence for it

16.pericope_label: Because that he remembered not to shew mercy, but persecuted the poor and needy man

debates.q: Whose words are the curses of these verses?

sides.view: The enemies’ own — the twentieth verse says this is their work, and so frees the psalm of every difficulty
The word may mean work or wages; the Greek and Latin take the former, but no conclusion is drawn
The psalmist’s, and a just recompense for hatred shown to Christ

debates.q: What is the curse that enters like water and oil?

sides.view: Perhaps the bitter waters of jealousy; and a girdle binding all mischief to the man
A medical figure: water in the belly and oil in the bone are both fatal
Wrath surrounding him and as visible as clothing

outliers.view: Claims the twentieth verse as the key that turns the imprecations into the enemies’ curses, on the ground that they sound more like the wicked than the inspired
Breaks off to describe a silver waist-chain from Ceylon lying on his desk as he writes

21.pericope_label: But do thou for me, O GOD the Lord, for thy name’s sake

debates.q: What is asked in the words do thou for me?

sides.view: Nothing specific — the psalmist dictates nothing and pleads only the name
A blessing set directly against the cursing of his enemies
The emphasis is untranslatable, and lies in the sudden turn from cursing to prayer
The prayer of Christ as man, that God would take his part

debates.q: What is the tossing like a locust?

sides.view: Shaken out, as from the lap; the insect is an emblem of timidity
Swarms driven upon each other by a brisk wind, as travellers describe
The violence of a life made to go, not merely going

outliers.view: Assembles three classical witnesses — Greek epic, Latin comedy and philosophical poem — to show that hunger is felt first in the knees and the eyes

26.pericope_label: Help me, O LORD my God: O save me according to thy mercy

debates.q: What is asked in let them curse, but bless thou?

sides.view: Three readings are open, including be thou blessed — if God blesses, cursing men matter nothing
Further proof that the curses of the psalm belong to the enemies, not the psalmist

debates.q: Who stands at the right hand of the poor?

sides.view: The Lord as advocate, answering the adversary who stood as accuser
God vindicating his servant even against Satan, as the resurrection vindicated Christ
Both the Messiah and his poor people

outliers.view: Reads the closing verse as the exact reversal of the psalm’s opening imprecation, with God taking the accuser’s station at the right hand
